title: Why Does Music Give You Chills?
subtitle: 音樂為什麼讓人起雞皮疙瘩？大腦的獎賞系統
source: 原創議題文章；依 Blood & Zatorre（PNAS, 2001）、Salimpoor et al.（Nature Neuroscience, 2011）、Sachs et al.（SCAN, 2016）摘要與 Wikipedia〈Frisson〉核對，2026-10-22

sources.title: Blood, A. J. & Zatorre, R. J. (2001). Intensely pleasurable responses to music correlate with activity in brain regions implicated in reward and emotion. PNAS 98(20), 11818–11823.
Salimpoor, V. N. et al. (2011). Anatomically distinct dopamine release during anticipation and experience of peak emotion to music. Nature Neuroscience 14, 257–262.
Sachs, M. E. et al. (2016). Brain connectivity reflects human aesthetic responses to music. Social Cognitive and Affective Neuroscience 11(6), 884–891.
Charles Darwin, The Descent of Man (1871), Project Gutenberg

beginner.title: A Shiver Down Your Spine
paras: You are listening to your favourite song. The music builds up, the singer hits a high note, and suddenly you feel a shiver down your back. The hair on your arms stands up. You have goosebumps! Many people have felt this. But why does music do this to us?
你正在聽最喜歡的歌。音樂漸漸堆高，歌手唱到一個高音，突然你感到背脊一陣發涼，手臂上的寒毛都豎了起來。你起雞皮疙瘩了！很多人都有過這種感覺。但為什麼音樂會讓我們這樣？

Scientists call this feeling “frisson”, a French word that means “shiver”. People can also feel it when they watch a film, hear a story or see something beautiful. Music is one of the most common causes. It often happens when something in the music surprises us.
科學家把這種感覺叫作 frisson，這是法文，意思是「顫抖」。人們在看電影、聽故事或看到美麗的事物時，也可能有這種感覺。音樂是最常見的原因之一。它常常發生在音樂裡有某個東西讓我們驚喜的時候。

In 2001, two scientists in Canada scanned people’s brains while they listened to music that gave them chills. The stronger the chills, the more active certain brain areas became. These areas are part of the brain’s “reward system”. They also become active when we eat good food. When people felt chills, their heart rate and breathing also changed.
2001 年，加拿大的兩位科學家在人們聆聽會讓他們起雞皮疙瘩的音樂時，掃描他們的大腦。雞皮疙瘩越強烈，某些腦區就越活躍。這些區域屬於大腦的「獎賞系統」，我們吃到美食時，它們也會活躍起來。人們起雞皮疙瘩時，心跳和呼吸也會改變。

Ten years later, another study found that the brain releases dopamine, a chemical linked to pleasure, during the best moments of a song. Amazingly, dopamine was also released just before those moments, while people were waiting for them. This may explain why we love waiting for our favourite part of a song.
十年後，另一項研究發現，在一首歌最精彩的時刻，大腦會釋放多巴胺——一種與愉悅感有關的化學物質。令人驚訝的是，在那些時刻來臨之前、人們正在期待的時候，大腦也會釋放多巴胺。這或許能解釋，為什麼我們那麼喜歡等待一首歌裡最愛的段落。

Not everyone gets chills from music. Some people get them often, and others almost never. One study found that people who get chills may have stronger connections between brain areas for hearing and areas for emotion. Do you get chills? Which song gives them to you?
不是每個人聽音樂都會起雞皮疙瘩。有些人常常有，有些人幾乎從來沒有。一項研究發現，會起雞皮疙瘩的人，大腦中負責聽覺的區域和負責情緒的區域之間，連結可能比較強。你會起雞皮疙瘩嗎？哪一首歌會讓你這樣？

intermediate.title: Why Does Music Give You Chills?
paras: A melody rises, the drums drop out, a voice soars — and a shiver runs down your spine. The skin on your arms turns to goosebumps. This experience has a name: frisson, from the French word for “shiver”. It is also called “aesthetic chills”, because it can be triggered by films, stories, rituals and beautiful scenes as well as by music.
旋律升高、鼓聲忽然停下、歌聲直衝雲霄——一股寒意沿著背脊竄下，手臂上的皮膚冒出雞皮疙瘩。這種經驗有個名字：frisson，源自法文的「顫抖」。它也被稱為「美感寒顫」，因為除了音樂，電影、故事、儀式和美麗的景色也都能引發它。

Researchers have found that chills are often linked to moments when music breaks our expectations. A sudden change in loudness, an unexpected harmony, a shift to a new key or a note that is unusually high or low can all activate the autonomic nervous system, which controls automatic body responses such as heart rate and breathing.
研究者發現，寒顫常與音樂打破我們預期的時刻有關。音量突然改變、意料之外的和聲、轉到新的調，或是一個特別高或特別低的音，都可能啟動自律神經系統——負責心跳、呼吸等自動身體反應的系統。

In 2001, Anne Blood and Robert Zatorre at McGill University used brain scanning to study listeners who had chosen music that gave them chills. As the chills grew stronger, activity changed in brain regions involved in reward, emotion and arousal — the same circuits that respond to food and other powerful rewards. In other words, the brain seems to treat a great piece of music almost like something it needs. The listeners’ bodies changed too: their heart rate, muscle activity and breathing all shifted as the chills came.
2001 年，麥基爾大學的安妮．布拉德和羅伯特．札托雷用腦部掃描，研究那些自選了會讓他們起雞皮疙瘩的音樂的聆聽者。隨著寒顫越來越強，與獎賞、情緒和激發有關的腦區活動也隨之改變——這些正是會對食物等強烈獎賞產生反應的迴路。換句話說，大腦似乎把一首好音樂，當成幾乎像是它需要的東西。聆聽者的身體也有變化：寒顫出現時，他們的心跳、肌肉活動和呼吸都改變了。

A 2011 study from the same university went further. Using two kinds of scans, the researchers found that dopamine was released in the brain at moments of peak emotion during music. Different parts of the brain were active in two stages: one during the anticipation of a favourite moment, and another when the moment actually arrived. The waiting itself, it seems, is part of the pleasure. The researchers suggested that this helps explain why music is so highly valued in every human society.
同一所大學 2011 年的一項研究更進一步。研究人員用兩種掃描方式發現，在聆聽音樂情緒達到高峰的時刻，大腦會釋放多巴胺。大腦的不同部位分兩個階段活躍：一個在期待最愛段落的時候，另一個在那一刻真正到來的時候。看來，等待本身就是愉悅的一部分。研究人員認為，這有助於解釋為什麼音樂在每個人類社會中都備受重視。

Yet people differ greatly. A 2016 study found that those who often experience chills tend to have stronger white matter connections between brain areas for processing sound and areas for emotion and social processing. Chills are also associated with the personality trait of openness to experience. So if music rarely gives you goosebumps, there is nothing wrong with you — your brain may simply be wired a little differently.
然而，人與人之間的差異很大。2016 年的一項研究發現，常起寒顫的人，大腦中處理聲音的區域與處理情緒、社交的區域之間，白質連結往往比較強。寒顫也與「對經驗開放」這種人格特質有關。所以，如果音樂很少讓你起雞皮疙瘩，你並沒有什麼問題——你的大腦只是接線方式稍有不同。

advanced.title: Anticipation, Reward and the Puzzle of Musical Pleasure
paras: Music presents an evolutionary puzzle. It provides no food, shelter or obvious survival advantage, yet it is found in every human society and can produce responses as intense as those triggered by tangible rewards. Charles Darwin, writing in The Descent of Man, ranked the enjoyment and production of music among the most mysterious faculties with which humans are endowed. One of its most vivid effects is frisson, or aesthetic chills: a shiver down the spine, often accompanied by goosebumps, in response to a powerful piece of music.
音樂是一個演化之謎。它不提供食物、居所或明顯的生存優勢，卻存在於每一個人類社會，而且能引發與有形獎賞一樣強烈的反應。查爾斯．達爾文在《人類的由來》中，把享受與創作音樂列為人類所具備的最神祕的能力之一。音樂最鮮明的效應之一，是 frisson，也就是美感寒顫：聽到一段動人的音樂時，背脊竄過一陣顫慄，常伴隨雞皮疙瘩。

Chills are frequently associated with violations of musical expectation. Sudden changes in dynamics, unexpected harmonies, modulations to new keys and notes at the extremes of pitch have all been shown to arouse the autonomic nervous system, and activation of that system correlates strongly with frisson. The phenomenon thus appears to depend on prediction: the brain constantly anticipates what will come next, and a well-placed surprise produces a physical response.
寒顫常與違反音樂預期有關。力度的突然變化、意料之外的和聲、轉調，以及音高位於極端的音符，都已被證明會激發自律神經系統，而這個系統的活化與寒顫高度相關。因此，這個現象似乎取決於預測：大腦不斷預期接下來會發生什麼，而一個恰到好處的驚喜，就會引發生理反應。

The neural basis of this pleasure was first mapped in 2001 by Anne Blood and Robert Zatorre at McGill University. Using positron emission tomography, they measured changes in cerebral blood flow while participants listened to self-selected music that reliably gave them chills. As the intensity of the chills increased, activity rose or fell in regions associated with reward, emotion and arousal, including the ventral striatum, midbrain, amygdala and orbitofrontal cortex — structures also engaged by food and other euphoria-inducing stimuli. Subjective reports of chills were accompanied by measurable changes in heart rate, muscle activity and respiration, confirming that the experience was physiological as well as emotional.

這種愉悅的神經基礎，最早在 2001 年由麥基爾大學的安妮．布拉德和羅伯特．札托雷描繪出來。他們用正子斷層掃描，在參與者聆聽自選、總能讓他們起寒顫的音樂時，測量腦血流的變化。隨著寒顫強度增加，與獎賞、情緒和激發相關的區域——包括腹側紋狀體、中腦、杏仁核和眼眶額葉皮質——活動隨之升高或降低；這些結構同樣會被食物等引發欣快感的刺激所啟動。受試者回報寒顫的同時，心跳、肌肉活動和呼吸也出現了可測量的變化，證實這種經驗不只是情緒上的，也是生理上的。

A decade later, Valorie Salimpoor and colleagues provided chemical evidence. Combining a PET technique sensitive to dopamine with functional MRI, they found that dopamine was released in the striatum at moments of peak emotional arousal. Crucially, they observed a functional dissociation: the caudate was more involved during the anticipation of a peak, and the nucleus accumbens during the experience of the peak itself. Pleasure in music, in other words, comes in two stages — the craving and the reward — each with its own neural pathway. An earlier preliminary study had even found that blocking the brain’s opioid receptors reduced or prevented chills in some listeners.

十年後，瓦萊麗．薩林普爾與同事提供了化學證據。他們結合對多巴胺敏感的正子掃描技術與功能性磁振造影，發現在情緒激發達到高峰的時刻，紋狀體會釋放多巴胺。關鍵在於，他們觀察到一種功能上的分離：尾狀核在期待高峰時較活躍，而依核則在體驗高峰本身時較活躍。換句話說，音樂帶來的愉悅分成兩個階段——渴望與獎賞——各有自己的神經路徑。更早的一項初步研究甚至發現，阻斷大腦的鴉片類受體，會讓部分聆聽者的寒顫減弱或消失。

Individual differences remain striking. Some listeners experience chills frequently; others rarely or never. In 2016, Sachs and colleagues reported that white matter connectivity between auditory regions in the superior temporal gyrus and emotional and social processing regions in the insula and medial prefrontal cortex helped explain these differences. The authors suggested that music’s power may derive from its role in social and emotional communication through sound. If so, Darwin’s mystery may have a partial answer: music moves us because it speaks to the parts of the brain built for connecting with others.
個體差異仍然非常明顯。有些聆聽者常起寒顫，有些很少甚至從不。2016 年，薩克斯與同事指出，位於顳上回的聽覺區，與位於腦島和內側前額葉皮質的情緒及社交處理區之間的白質連結，有助於解釋這些差異。作者認為，音樂的力量可能來自它透過聲音進行社交與情感溝通的角色。若是如此，達爾文的謎題或許有了部分答案：音樂之所以打動我們，是因為它對大腦中為了與他人連結而生的部分說話。

quote.text: As neither the enjoyment nor the capacity of producing musical notes are faculties of the least use to man in reference to his daily habits of life, they must be ranked amongst the most mysterious with which he is endowed.
quote.author: Charles Darwin

beginner.q: What is the passage mainly about?
options: Why only French people are able to feel frisson.
How to sing a high note without feeling nervous.
Why music gives people chills and what the brain does.
How to make your favourite song sound much louder.
beginner.evidence: But why does music do this to us?
beginner.why: 全文：音樂帶來寒顫的原因與大腦機制。
traps: 字面誤讀：frisson 只是法文借字。
以偏概全：高音只是開頭的情境。
捏造：文中沒談音量操作。

beginner.q: What does “those moments” in the fourth paragraph refer to?
options: The best moments of a song.
The moments when people eat good food.
The times when people feel afraid.
The ten years between the two studies.
beginner.evidence: the brain releases dopamine, a chemical linked to pleasure, during the best moments of a song
beginner.why: 前一句：歌曲最精彩的時刻。
traps: 原文字眼、錯誤關係：食物是第三段比較的例子。
捏造：文中沒有談恐懼。
原文字眼、錯誤關係：十年是兩項研究的間隔。

beginner.q: Which of the following is true according to the passage?
options: Chills happen only when people listen to music.
The 2001 study took place in France.
Everyone gets chills from music in the same way.
Dopamine was released even while people waited for their favourite part.
beginner.evidence: dopamine was also released just before those moments, while people were waiting for them
traps: 以偏概全：看電影、聽故事也會。
張冠李戴：研究在加拿大，法文只是 frisson 的字源。
正反顛倒：有人常有，有人幾乎沒有。

beginner.q: What might explain why some people get chills more often?
options: They eat more good food than other people.
Stronger connections between brain areas for hearing and emotion.
They listen to music only in French.
They have never heard a surprising song.
beginner.evidence: people who get chills may have stronger connections between brain areas for hearing and areas for emotion
traps: 原文字眼、錯誤關係：食物只是說明大腦獎勵系統的例子。
字面誤讀：frisson 只是名稱。
正反顛倒：寒顫常來自音樂中的驚喜。

intermediate.q: Which of the following best states the main idea of the passage?
options: People who rarely get chills have something wrong with them.
Only music can give people chills or goosebumps.
Dopamine is released only after a song has ended.
Musical chills come from surprise and the brain’s reward system, and people differ.
intermediate.evidence: The waiting itself, it seems, is part of the pleasure.
intermediate.why: 第二到五段：驚喜觸發寒顫、獎勵系統與多巴胺、個別差異。
traps: 正反顛倒：原文 there is nothing wrong with you。
正反顛倒：電影、故事、儀式也會。
時序錯置：期待和高潮時都會釋放。

intermediate.q: What does the “autonomic nervous system” control, according to the passage?
options: Our ability to choose our favourite songs.
Automatic body responses such as heart rate and breathing.
The muscles we use to play instruments.
The memories we have of old music.
intermediate.evidence: which controls automatic body responses such as heart rate and breathing
intermediate.why: 第二段的關係子句直接說明。
traps: 正反顛倒：它控制的是「自動」反應，不是選擇。
捏造：文中沒有。這不是自主神經的功能。
捏造：文中沒談記憶。

intermediate.q: Which of the following is true according to the passage?
options: Chills are linked to the personality trait of shyness.
The 2011 study was carried out at a university in France.
Listeners in the 2001 study chose music that gave them chills.
Heart rate stayed the same during the chills.
intermediate.evidence: used brain scanning to study listeners who had chosen music that gave them chills
traps: 張冠李戴：相關的是「對經驗開放」。
張冠李戴：2011 年的研究也在 McGill（加拿大）。
正反顛倒：心跳、呼吸都改變了。

intermediate.q: What does the two-stage finding in the 2011 study suggest?
options: Waiting for a favourite moment is itself part of the pleasure.
Music stops being enjoyable after the first stage.
Only the final moment of a song matters.
People cannot enjoy music they already know.
intermediate.evidence: The waiting itself, it seems, is part of the pleasure.
traps: 捏造：文中沒說樂趣會在第一階段後消失。
正反顛倒：期待階段也有作用。
捏造：參與者聽的正是自己喜歡的音樂。

advanced.q: What is the main purpose of the passage?
options: To explain the brain mechanisms behind musical chills and why people differ.
To argue that music has no value for human survival.
To describe Darwin’s life and travels.
To teach readers how to compose surprising music.
advanced.evidence: Darwin’s mystery may have a partial answer
advanced.why: 全文：從達爾文的謎題出發，說明大腦機制與個別差異。
traps: 過度推論：作者說它沒有明顯的生存好處，但最後提出可能的社會功能。
以偏概全：達爾文只在開頭和結尾出現。
捏造：文中沒有教作曲。

advanced.q: Which of the following is closest in meaning to “dissociation” in the fourth paragraph?
options: A sudden loss of hearing.
A friendly link between two people.
A clear separation between two processes.
A rise in heart rate.
advanced.evidence: the caudate was more involved during the anticipation of a peak, and the nucleus accumbens during the experience of the peak itself
advanced.why: 冒號後面說明：期待和體驗由不同腦區負責，彼此分開。
traps: 捏造：文中沒提到聽力喪失。
字面誤讀：association 有交往之意，這裡是「分離」。
原文字眼、錯誤關係：心跳變化是第三段的身體反應。

advanced.q: Which of the following is true according to the passage?
options: Blood and Zatorre used functional MRI in 2001.
Blocking opioid receptors reduced or prevented chills in some listeners.
Salimpoor found dopamine released only during anticipation.
Sachs and colleagues published their study in 2001.
advanced.evidence: blocking the brain’s opioid receptors reduced or prevented chills in some listeners
traps: 張冠李戴：2001 年用的是 PET。
以偏概全：期待和高潮時都有。
數字錯位：2016 年。

advanced.q: How does the author suggest Darwin’s mystery might be partly answered?
options: Music is found only in a few societies.
Music provides food and shelter for listeners.
Music was invented by Darwin himself.
Music engages brain systems built for connecting with others.
advanced.evidence: music moves us because it speaks to the parts of the brain built for connecting with others
traps: 正反顛倒：每個人類社會都有音樂。
正反顛倒：音樂不提供食物或住所。
捏造：達爾文是提出謎題的人。

reflections: Choose a song that gives you chills. At what exact moment does it happen? Can you explain it using the idea of “broken expectations”?
Darwin thought music was mysterious because it seems useless for survival. Do you agree? What might music be “for”?

paras: Music presents a puzzle. It provides no food or shelter, yet it is found in every human society and can produce responses as intense as those caused by real rewards. Charles Darwin, writing in The Descent of Man, counted the enjoyment of music among the most mysterious abilities humans have. One of its most vivid effects is frisson, or aesthetic chills: a shiver down the spine, often with goosebumps, in response to a powerful piece of music.
音樂是一個謎。它不提供食物或住所，卻存在於每一個人類社會，而且能引發和真正的獎賞一樣強烈的反應。達爾文在《人類的由來》中，把欣賞音樂列為人類最神秘的能力之一。音樂最鮮明的效果之一是「顫慄」，也叫審美寒顫：聽到一段強而有力的音樂時，背脊竄過一陣顫抖，常伴隨著雞皮疙瘩。

Chills are often linked to moments when music breaks our expectations. Sudden changes in loudness, unexpected harmonies, shifts to a new key and notes that are unusually high or low can all activate the autonomic nervous system, which controls automatic body responses such as heart rate and breathing. So closely is this system linked to the music that its activity strongly predicts frisson. The brain, it seems, keeps predicting what will come next, and a well-placed surprise produces a physical response.
寒顫常和音樂打破我們預期的時刻有關。音量突然改變、意料之外的和聲、轉到新的調，以及異常高或低的音，都可能啟動自主神經系統——它控制心跳、呼吸等自動的身體反應。這個系統的活動和寒顫緊密相連，能有力地預測寒顫的出現。看來，大腦不斷預測接下來會發生什麼，而一個恰到好處的驚喜，就會帶來身體反應。

The brain basis of this pleasure was first mapped in 2001 by Anne Blood and Robert Zatorre at McGill University. Using brain scans, they studied listeners who had chosen music that reliably gave them chills. As the chills grew stronger, activity changed in regions linked to reward, emotion and arousal — the same areas that respond to food and other powerful rewards. The listeners’ heart rate, muscle activity and breathing also changed, showing that the experience was physical as well as emotional.
這種愉悅的大腦基礎，最早在 2001 年由麥基爾大學的布拉德和札托雷繪製出來。他們用腦部掃描，研究那些自選了總能讓自己起寒顫的音樂的聽者。寒顫越強，和獎賞、情緒、興奮有關的腦區活動就越有變化——這些腦區也會對食物和其他強烈的獎賞起反應。聽者的心跳、肌肉活動和呼吸也都改變了，顯示這種體驗既是情緒的，也是生理的。

A decade later, Valorie Salimpoor and her colleagues provided chemical evidence. They found that dopamine (a brain chemical linked to pleasure) was released at moments of peak emotion. One part of the brain was more involved while listeners waited for a favourite moment, and another when the moment actually arrived. It is in two stages that pleasure in music comes: the craving and the reward. An earlier small study had even found that blocking certain brain receptors reduced or prevented chills in some listeners.
十年後，薩林波和同事提出了化學證據。他們發現，在情緒最高漲的時刻，大腦會釋放多巴胺（一種和愉悅有關的大腦化學物質）。聽者等待最愛的段落時，某個腦區比較活躍；那一刻真正來臨時，則是另一個腦區。所以，音樂帶來的愉悅分成兩個階段：渴望和獎賞。更早的一項小型研究甚至發現，阻斷某些大腦受體，能減少或阻止部分聽者起寒顫。

Yet people differ greatly. Some listeners feel chills often; others rarely or never. In 2016, Matthew Sachs and colleagues reported that stronger connections between brain areas for processing sound and areas for emotion and social processing helped explain these differences. The authors suggested that music’s power may come from its role in social and emotional communication. If so, Darwin’s mystery may have a partial answer: music moves us because it speaks to the parts of the brain built for connecting with others.
然而人和人之間差異很大：有些人常起寒顫，有些人很少或從來沒有。2016 年，薩克斯和同事報告，處理聲音的腦區與處理情緒和社交的腦區之間連結較強，有助於解釋這些差異。作者認為，音樂的力量可能來自它在社交與情緒溝通上的角色。若真是如此，達爾文的謎題或許有了部分答案：音樂之所以打動我們，是因為它對大腦中為了與他人連結而生的部分說話。

questions.q: What is the passage mainly about?
options: Why only some songs are found in every society.
How Charles Darwin learned to play music.
What happens in the brain when music gives people chills.
How to make goosebumps disappear quickly.
questions.evidence: The brain basis of this pleasure was first mapped in 2001
questions.why: 全文：音樂寒顫的觸發、大腦機制與個別差異。
traps: 正反顛倒：是「音樂」存在於每個社會，不是某些歌曲。
捏造：達爾文只是提出這個謎題。
捏造：文中沒有教人消除雞皮疙瘩。

questions.q: What does “its activity” in the second paragraph refer to?
options: The activity of the autonomic nervous system.
The activity of the listeners’ favourite song.
The activity of people in every society.
The activity of Charles Darwin’s research.
questions.evidence: So closely is this system linked to the music that its activity strongly predicts frisson.
questions.why: its 指同一句的 this system，也就是自主神經系統。
traps: 原文字眼、錯誤關係：音樂是被追蹤的對象。
時序錯置：每個社會是第一段的內容。
時序錯置：達爾文在第一段。

questions.q: Which of the following is true according to the passage?
options: Blood and Zatorre worked at a university in France.
Dopamine was released only after the music had ended.
Everyone feels musical chills equally often.
Listeners in the 2001 study chose music that gave them chills.
questions.evidence: they studied listeners who had chosen music that reliably gave them chills
traps: 張冠李戴：他們在麥基爾大學，法文只是 frisson 的字源。
時序錯置：在情緒最高峰時釋放。
正反顛倒：原文說人和人差異很大。

questions.q: What can be inferred from the two-stage finding in the fourth paragraph?
options: Music stops being enjoyable after the first stage.
Waiting for a favourite moment is itself part of the pleasure.
Only the final note of a song matters.
People cannot enjoy music they already know.
questions.evidence: One part of the brain was more involved while listeners waited for a favourite moment
questions.why: 等待時也有腦區參與，可推知期待本身就是愉悅的一部分。
traps: 捏造：文中沒有。第二階段是獎賞。
正反顛倒：期待階段也有作用。
捏造：聽者選的正是自己喜歡的音樂。

Blood and Zatorre published their study in 2011.
